title: Protecting the Shop: Card Data, Account Takeover, Bots and Skimmers
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/34-commerce-security/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for that the published chapter did not have: a roadmap p05 that announces every section and a conclusion paragraph p56 that answers the opening; see decision_log.

know: What attackers take from a shop, in rough order of preference: card testing, credential stuffing and account takeover, web skimming, coupon and refund abuse, inventory hoarding, admin compromise and supply-chain risk, with OWASP identifiers where they exist; half of them policy abuse rather than intrusion.

Where PCI DSS draws its line: the SAQ by integration pattern (a PSP-hosted page or hosted fields for SAQ A, a merchant form for SAQ A-EP, raw card data for SAQ D), the dates of v4.0 and v4.0.1, requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 mandatory since 31 March 2025 and removed from SAQ A in favor of an eligibility statement, and requirements 12.8 and 8.4.2.

The controls for card testing (the control ladder up to a decline-rate alert and a kill switch), for takeover (rate limits, challenges for risky logins, notification of change), for skimmers (script inventory, CSP, SRI, tamper detection) and for identities (enforced MFA, one restricted key per integration in a vault, signed webhooks), and the four security postures by scale stage.
believe: Attackers do not break in; they use the payment form, the login and the admin as built.
The hosted platform removes the patching burden and never the identity, script and endpoint burden.
For a merchant renting its platform, security is an inventory of identities, keys, apps, scripts and endpoints with owners before it is a technology.
can_do: Place their checkout on the SAQ table and say what the SAQ A eligibility statement asks them to know about the scripts on their payment page.
Audit their landscape as a list of identities and keys, each with an owner, a scope and a way to rotate it, and move one posture rung when the landscape gains what the rung protects.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or product manager who inherits a storefront with an agency, apps and integrations and is asked "are we secure?" (Milan Petrov and Noor Visser at Kestrel & Pine); next, the finance or operations lead who sees PSP fees for declined payments or a paused account, and the architect choosing between a hosted checkout and a custom one.
already_knows: Roughly what an API, a database, a login and a web page's scripts are.

Kestrel & Pine, its people (Noor Visser, Milan Petrov), its 2026 and January 2027 incidents in outline (including the Card-Testing Night and the Double Refund), the sixteen failure-pattern names and the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II to VI: checkout creating the order once with payment pending until the provider's signed message; authorization, capture, settlement, refunds as new payments; an integration inventory with an owner per flow (13 of 34 integrations unowned in January 2027).

From Part VII: the vendor's inside reaches the merchant as limits (API budgets, dated extension points, a checkout it cannot replace); promises are kept or broken in the merchant's own layer; app governance with an owner, scopes and API version per app; orders per minute as the peak health signal.

From the Part VIII introduction: a checkout that accepts a real purchase also accepts 48,000 attempts with stolen cards by the same behavior; each chapter of the part adds a column to the ownership map, this one credentials with their owners.
does_not_know: Card testing, credential stuffing, account takeover, web skimming, inventory hoarding, scraping, OWASP and its automated-threat identifiers.
PCI DSS, acquirer, PAN, SAQ (A, A-EP, D), hosted fields, token, attestation of compliance, requirements 6.4.3, 11.6.1, 12.8 and 8.4.2.

CSP, SRI, tamper detection, MFA, passkey, restricted key, secrets vault, bot management, rate limit, velocity rule, kill switch, decline rate, dunning, shared responsibility, SCA and 3-D Secure in one clause.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an overnight wave of declined payments on a hosted platform, the reader names the attack and the controls that stop it, rather than relying on the platform's certification or an IP block.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant on a hosted platform with a hosted checkout wakes to payment-provider fees for tens of thousands of declined authorizations made overnight through its guest checkout, a payment account paused for 40 minutes, and a few hundred real orders with nonsense names. Its agency says the platform is PCI certified, so security is handled, and proposes blocking the IP addresses involved. Using only this chapter: what happened, and what should the merchant put in place?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Card testing (OAT-001): a script used the guest checkout as built to find which stolen cards still work. Every attempt is a normal checkout to the platform and a normal authorization to the PSP, so only the count, pace and decline rate reveal it; attackers rotate addresses, so an IP block is not enough, and the certification covers the vendor's service, not abuse of the merchant's endpoints. Controls: keep the hosted checkout; switch on the platform's bot protection and the PSP's velocity rules; challenge payment requests with no session history, validated on the server; alert on the decline rate against normal; keep a kill switch that disables guest card payments without a deploy; never retry the cards the attacker saved; write a runbook that calls a named person. In the response: cancel and refund the live orders before they reach the warehouse, and rotate every key if the attempts did not come through the checkout.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say how much of PCI DSS applies to a merchant with hosted fields and what it still owns on the payment page.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant takes cards through its PSP's hosted fields inside its own checkout page, which also loads a tag manager and two app scripts. Using only this chapter: how much of PCI DSS applies to it, and what does it still own?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The card number goes from the shopper's browser straight to the PSP and the merchant holds only a token, the brand, the last four digits and the expiry, so SAQ A can apply if its eligibility criteria are met; the acquirer, not a vendor's documentation, decides the SAQ. Requirements 6.4.3 (every payment-page script authorized, integrity-checked and inventoried with a reason) and 11.6.1 (detect and alert on unauthorized page and header changes) are mandatory in the standard since 31 March 2025; the Council removed them from SAQ A but asks an SAQ A merchant to confirm that its site is not susceptible to script attacks, which it can do itself, through a third party or with the processor's confirmation. So the merchant keeps a script inventory with an owner and a reason, a CSP in report-only and then enforcing mode, SRI on the PSP's scripts and tamper detection; holds each provider's attestation (12.8); and enforces MFA on the PSP console and the platform admin (8.4.2, as the chapter reads it). A custom card form would move it to SAQ A-EP or SAQ D.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what a merchant's list of identities and keys should hold and why.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant's platform admin has about thirty staff accounts, some shared and MFA optional; its agency uses one shared login; and it runs dozens of integrations whose keys sit in scripts and never rotate, some with no named owner. Using only this chapter: what should change, and why does it matter more than another security product?
acceptance_criteria.expected: An admin login or a leaked key bypasses every other control: it can change the payout account, add a checkout script, export customers or issue refunds, and the vendor's shared-responsibility statement leaves identities, keys, apps, scripts and integrations to the merchant. So: MFA enforced, not merely available, on the platform, the PSP console, the ERP, the WMS and the integration platform; no shared accounts, agency engineers named, leavers removed within a day; one identity and one restricted, least-privilege key per integration, with an owner in the inventory, held in a vault and rotated yearly or on exposure; webhook signatures verified; app scopes reviewed before installation. A key without an owner cannot be rotated, scoped or traced, and a merchant that cannot say which integration a leaked key belonged to must rotate everything.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a checkout accepting strangers' payments can be used to test stolen cards, a login to try stolen passwords and bot carts to hold stock, with no break-in; the damage as fees for declined payments, a paused payment account, stolen customer access, held stock and, from malicious checkout scripts, stolen card details (British Airways, 2018, with a £20 million penalty in 2020); that a merchant renting its platform still holds access, integrations, custom scripts and abuse controls; that the chapter covers payment-page exposure, card testing and account takeover and leaves personal data, the wider rules and fraud models to other chapters; Eva paying by iDEAL at a checkout that took 48,000 abusive attempts one night. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Card-Testing Night and its 2027 baseline, vendor documentation (Stripe, Adyen, Shopify, Adobe), the PCI Security Standards Council, OWASP and dated public breaches.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What do attackers want from a commerce platform, and what controls matter most?
thesis.claim: Attackers want the payment form, the login and the admin, and send ordinary requests through them as designed rather than break in. For a merchant renting its platform the controls that matter most are a hosted checkout that keeps card numbers out of its systems; challenges, rate limits and a decline-rate alert on every endpoint that can pay or log in; an owned inventory of checkout scripts; and one identity, scoped key and named owner per person, app and integration.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that on a hosted, PCI-certified platform security is the vendor's job, so the merchant's part is a firewall or a bot-management product, and card testing is stopped by blocking the IP addresses it comes from.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim keeps its checkout hosted, switches on the controls it already pays for, watches the decline rate beside the order rate, keeps its checkout scripts on a list, and gives every identity and key an owner who can rotate it. On the night of 18 to 19 August 2026 a script made 48,000 guest-checkout attempts on Kestrel & Pine's NL storefront between about 23:40 and 04:10; the PSP charged €2,900 in fees for declined authorizations and paused the account for 40 minutes from 02:05, with its e-mail unread until 07:30; about 260 cards were live, 21 orders came back as disputes, and the issuer decline rate on genuine card payments rose from about 4% to about 7% for two weeks. At the time the platform had 31 admin accounts (4 shared, MFA optional), keys sat in scripts and the integration platform and were never rotated, and 13 of 34 integrations had no named owner in January 2027 (5 were still unowned in April 2027). The April 2027 baseline confirmed SAQ A with the acquirer, added a challenge on session-less payment requests, a decline-rate alert at three times the 30-day median, a guest-card kill switch tested quarterly, enforced MFA with no shared accounts, one identity and restricted key per integration in a vault, a checkout script inventory with CSP enforcing from September 2027, and three runbooks.
thesis.how_why: Card testing and credential stuffing send normal requests to the checkout and the login from rotating addresses, so a single filter fails and only the count, the pace and the decline rate reveal them; the PSP charges for every authorization, pauses accounts that look abused, and issuers decline more of the merchant's genuine payments afterwards. A hosted checkout or hosted fields sends the card number straight to the PSP, which puts the merchant in SAQ A, but a skimmer runs in the shopper's browser on a page the merchant serves, which is why PCI DSS requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 apply since 31 March 2025 and SAQ A asks the merchant to state that its page is not susceptible to script attacks. An admin login or a leaked key needs no other technique, and the vendors' published shared-responsibility statements (Adobe, Shopify, Stripe) leave identities, keys, apps, scripts and integrations to the merchant, so a key with no owner is a door nobody can close.

supporting_claims.claim: Attackers do not break in: card testing, credential stuffing, coupon and refund abuse and inventory hoarding send ordinary requests through the payment form, the login, the cart and the merchant's own rules, so only the count, the pace and the decline rate reveal them and the controls sit where the abused function lives.

The vendors' published shared-responsibility statements agree: the vendor secures, patches and certifies its service, and the merchant secures the identities, keys, apps, scripts and integrations it adds.

A hosted checkout or hosted fields keeps the card number out of the merchant's systems and puts it in SAQ A, but a skimmer runs in the shopper's browser on the merchant's page, so since 31 March 2025 the scripts on the payment page are the merchant's to inventory, or at least to vouch for in the SAQ A eligibility statement.

Card testing and account takeover are stopped by layered controls on every endpoint that can pay or log in (the hosted checkout's defaults, bot protection and velocity rules, a session requirement and risk-triggered challenges, MFA, a decline-rate alert and a kill switch), not by one filter or an IP block.

An admin login or a leaked key needs no other technique, so every person, app and integration gets its own identity, a narrow key in a vault and a named owner who can rotate it, with the posture raised one rung when the landscape gains what that rung protects.

role.contribution: Names what attackers take from a shop and where the card-data standard draws its line, and turns the merchant's side of shared responsibility into a list of identities, keys, scripts and endpoints, each with an owner, an alert and a runbook.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to in-practice: the August night and Noor's question first, the 2027 baseline that answers it last

flow.rationale: The night and Noor's question come first so every later section answers part of it. The threat list follows because it names the doors; shared responsibility follows because it says which of those doors the hosted platform already guards and which stay with the merchant; card data comes next because it is the first and largest decision in the merchant's share, and the skimmer section follows it because hosted fields leave the page around the fields exposed; that section gives the attack first and the standard's script requirements after it, so no rule waits for its reason. The attacks that use the shop's own doors follow (payment form, login and cart, then the admin and keys); the request-path requirements then gather the challenge, login and webhook controls of those three sections, the postures and the stage table size the controls, and the book's fixed closing order (in practice, when it goes wrong) applies them to Kestrel & Pine. Putting the controls before the threat list would give answers before the reader knows the doors; putting the script requirements before the skimmer attack sends the reader forward and lists the controls twice, which readers in two rounds found hard to follow. The cost of this order is that the scene's own attack, card testing, waits until after card data and skimmers; the reader accepts that because the card-testing controls build on the hosted checkout and the PSP that those sections introduce. Policy abuse (refunds and coupons) is settled inside the threat section because it needs no endpoint control, so When It Goes Wrong holds intrusions only.

hook.content: A checkout must accept payment attempts from strangers; an attacker uses that same behavior to test stolen cards, automated logins try stolen passwords and bot carts reserve stock, and the shop processes every request exactly as designed.

sections.heading: Shared Responsibility: What the Platform Does and What You Must Do
sections.controlling_idea: Vendors publish the line between their work and the merchant's: the vendor secures, patches and certifies its service, and the merchant secures the code, scripts, apps, accounts and keys it adds.

advances_thesis.how: States the vendor's and the merchant's shares from the vendors' own words.

flow.rationale: The division is asserted first, then three vendors' statements support it, then the reading of all three draws the line the rest of the chapter works on.

transition_in.carries_over: Threats whose controls sit on the merchant's functions.
transition_in.introduces: Which of those controls the hosted platform already provides.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Buying a hosted platform divides security work between vendor and merchant, because the vendor can secure its infrastructure while an unsafe app, an exposed key or a poorly managed staff account still opens a route into the shop.

Adobe's shared-responsibility model is the most explicit: Adobe keeps core code, operating system, firewall rules and infrastructure certification, and the merchant secures its custom code and integrations, applies patches, manages user access and handles its incidents.

evidence.what: The merchant secures "custom code and integrations with third-party applications".
evidence.source: Adobe Experience League, Shared responsibility, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: Shows a vendor naming the merchant's share in writing.

transition_in.introduces: The most explicit published version of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify states that its Level 1 PCI DSS certification extends to all stores by default while the merchant still has steps of its own.

evidence.what: "certified Level 1 PCI DSS compliant"; "extends by default to all stores powered by Shopify"; "there are also steps you will need to take on your own".
evidence.source: Shopify security and PCI pages, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: Shows a certification that covers the service, not the merchant's additions.

transition_in.introduces: Shopify's version.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe says the same about payments: PCI compliance is a shared responsibility of Stripe and the business.

transition_in.introduces: The payment provider's.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read together, the vendor covers the service's code, hosting, patching, certification and default tools, and the merchant covers what it adds, who holds an admin account and whether MFA is enforced, which keys exist and incident response: the hosted platform removes the patching burden and never the identity, script and endpoint burden.

sections.heading: Card Data: Where PCI DSS Draws Its Line
sections.controlling_idea: PCI DSS asks least of a merchant whose systems never see the card number, so the integration pattern sets how much of the standard applies, and two requirements (provider attestations and MFA) apply to every hosted merchant.

advances_thesis.how: Places each integration pattern on the SAQ table and states the script requirements and the SAQ A statement as the Council wrote them.

flow.rationale: From what the standard is and when it changed, to which questionnaire applies by integration pattern, to what card data the merchant may keep, to the two requirements every hosted merchant meets; the script requirements wait for the next section, after the attack they answer.

transition_in.carries_over: The vendor's certification covers its service.
transition_in.introduces: The standard that certification refers to and where it draws the merchant's line.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: PCI DSS is the card brands' contractual security standard, enforced through the acquirer, and a modern checkout's design goal is to keep its scope, the systems that touch card data, as small as possible, ideally none of the merchant's own.

The standard changed recently: v4.0 in March 2022, v3.2.1 retired 31 March 2024, v4.0.1 published 11 June 2024, v4.0 retired 31 December 2024, and the requirements v4.0 introduced as best practice mandatory since 31 March 2025.

evidence.what: The five dates.
evidence.source: PCI Security Standards Council blog, 11 June 2024
evidence.shows: Shows which version and which requirements apply now.

transition_in.introduces: Its recent dates.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: How much of the standard applies depends on how the card number reaches the PSP, because the self-assessment questionnaire follows the integration pattern, from SAQ A for a PSP-hosted page or hosted fields to SAQ D for raw card data, with the acquirer deciding.

evidence.what: Four integration patterns: who sees the card number, typical SAQ, what the merchant still owns.
evidence.source: Author's synthesis of Stripe's and Adyen's guides, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: Lets the reader place their own checkout.

transition_in.introduces: How much of it applies to a given checkout.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Hosted platforms with their own checkout put every merchant in the first two rows, which makes this the largest security decision a merchant makes, usually by default; a custom checkout that collects card numbers moves it down the table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The brand, last four digits and expiry may be stored, and everything else is replaced by a token the PSP issues to charge or refund the card again.

evidence.what: Stripe integration security guide, n.d.
evidence.shows: Supports what card data the merchant may keep.

transition_in.carries_over: The card number going straight to the PSP.
transition_in.introduces: What the merchant holds instead.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two requirements apply to every hosted merchant whatever its checkout: 12.8 makes it responsible for its service providers and their attestations, and 8.4.2 requires MFA for access into the cardholder-data environment, which for a hosted merchant means the PSP console and the platform admin.

evidence.what: "Adyen is solely responsible for the security of cardholder data only as soon as Adyen receives the data".
evidence.source: Adyen PCI DSS compliance guide, n.d.
evidence.shows: Shows where the provider's responsibility starts.

transition_in.carries_over: The card data a hosted merchant may keep.
transition_in.introduces: The two requirements every hosted merchant meets whatever its checkout.

sections.heading: Skimmers: The Attack in the Shopper's Browser
sections.controlling_idea: A skimmer runs in the shopper's browser on a page the merchant serves, through a stolen login, a third-party script or an unpatched flaw, and PCI DSS answers it with two script requirements that stay in the standard even where SAQ A asks only for a statement, so the page's scripts are the merchant's to know.

advances_thesis.how: Shows with dated public cases why the payment page's scripts are the merchant's, and states the script requirements and the SAQ A statement as the Council wrote them.

flow.rationale: The attack first (definition, the British Airways case and its lessons, the supply-chain cases), then the standard's answer (the two script requirements, their removal from SAQ A, what the statement means, the controls behind it), so every rule arrives after the attack that explains it and the controls are listed once.

transition_in.carries_over: Hosted fields that keep the card number out of the merchant's systems.
transition_in.introduces: The page around the fields, where a skimmer runs, and the requirements written for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Hosted fields keep the card number away from the merchant's systems but not from the page around the fields, where a web skimmer, malicious code that copies payment or personal data as the shopper types it, can steal data before the PSP receives it.

The British Airways breach of 2018 is the clearest public record: a third-party login without MFA, a saved privileged credential, 22 lines of JavaScript on the payment pages, about 429,612 people affected and a £20 million penalty in 2020.

evidence.what: BA: entry 22 June 2018; script 14 to 25 August 2018; about 429,612 people; ICO penalty £20 million on 16 October 2020.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, citing the ICO penalty notice, 2020
evidence.shows: Shows a skimmer's whole path from a misused login to stolen card data.

transition_in.introduces: The clearest public case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two lessons survive: the skimmer ran in the shopper's browser on a page the merchant served without breaking the PSP, and its entry was an identity, a third-party login without MFA.

transition_in.introduces: What it teaches a merchant today.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The supply-chain version needs no action by the merchant: Polyfill's compromised script reached more than 100,000 sites in 2024, and unpatched self-hosted stores were breached through CosmicSting the same year.

evidence.what: Polyfill: sold February 2024, reported 25 June 2024, more than 100,000 sites. CosmicSting (CVE-2024-34102): fixed 11 June 2024, thousands of unpatched stores breached in October and November.
evidence.source: Sansec, 2024
evidence.shows: Shows that a script or a patch the merchant does not control can expose its shoppers.

evidence.what: "Including JavaScript from other sites makes your security dependent on theirs."
evidence.source: Stripe integration security guide, n.d.
evidence.shows: States the principle in one sentence.

transition_in.carries_over: A skimmer added through a stolen login.
transition_in.introduces: Skimmers that arrive through third-party scripts and unpatched code.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: PCI DSS answers these attacks with two requirements on the page around the card fields, 6.4.3 (every payment-page script authorized, integrity-checked and inventoried with a reason) and 11.6.1 (detect and alert on unauthorized page and header changes), required since 31 March 2025.

evidence.what: PCI SSC, 26 March 2025.
evidence.shows: Supports the wording and the date of both requirements.

transition_in.carries_over: Skimmers that arrive through stolen logins, third-party scripts and unpatched code.
transition_in.introduces: The standard's two requirements on the page around the card fields.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Council removed 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 from SAQ A and added an eligibility criterion instead: the merchant confirms its site is not susceptible to script attacks, itself, through a third party or with its processor's confirmation.

evidence.what: "is not susceptible to attacks from scripts that could affect the merchant's e-commerce systems".
evidence.source: PCI SSC, 26 March 2025
evidence.shows: States the eligibility criterion in the Council's words.

transition_in.carries_over: The two requirements in the standard.
transition_in.introduces: Their removal from SAQ A and the eligibility statement that replaced it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The requirements remain in the standard, so a merchant on a hosted checkout no longer proves a script inventory but must state that its page cannot be skimmed and should know why the statement is true.

evidence.what: "these requirements were only removed from SAQ A, and they are still in the standard".
evidence.source: PCI SSC, 26 March 2025
evidence.shows: Shows the Council's own reading of the change.

transition_in.introduces: What it means for the merchant in plain words.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen's guidance describes the work behind the statement (a Content Security Policy in report-only then enforcing mode, an inventory with business reasons, Subresource Integrity on the PSP's scripts, violation reports as indicators of compromise, and tamper detection), and on a hosted platform the merchant's exposure is the scripts it adds through the theme, apps and tag managers.

evidence.what: Violation reports as "valid alerts and 'indicators of compromise'".
evidence.source: Adyen script security, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: Shows a PSP describing the controls behind the statement.

transition_in.carries_over: The statement the merchant must be able to back.
transition_in.introduces: The controls that back it.

sections.heading: Card Testing: The Attack and the Controls
sections.controlling_idea: Card testing looks like normal checkouts from rotating addresses, so it is stopped by a ladder of layered controls and a decline-rate alert, not by one filter.

advances_thesis.how: Explains the attack from the PSP's documentation and gives the control ladder with its budgets.

flow.rationale: The attack and why single filters fail come first; the ladder of controls answers it; the cost of false challenges then sets a limit on the ladder. The per-control requirements table is its own section after the identity section, because it also covers the login and webhook controls.

transition_in.carries_over: Skimmers, which steal card numbers as shoppers type them.
transition_in.introduces: The attack of the August night, which brings its own stolen cards and needs only a checkout that will try them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Unlike a skimmer, card testing needs none of the merchant's card data: it uses the payment or card-saving interface to discover which stolen cards still work, and the merchant pays in fees and disruption even when no genuine order results.

Stripe's documentation describes the attack: card saving preferred to payment because it does not show on statements, symptoms of failed payments, 402 responses and nonsense names, and a high decline rate damaging the merchant's standing with issuers.

evidence.what: "don't typically show up on cardholder statements"; "often with nonsensical customer names and emails"; "a high decline rate might damage the reputation of your business with card issuers and card networks".
evidence.source: Stripe, Protect yourself from card testing, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: Shows the mechanism and the lasting cost from the PSP's own description.

evidence.what: Figure 3: the night as a sequence of normal checkouts and authorizations.
evidence.shows: Shows that only count, pace and decline rate reveal the attack.

transition_in.introduces: How it works and what it looks like, from the PSP's documentation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Single filters such as IP blocks fail because attackers rotate addresses, and a leaked secret key lets testers create payments with no checkout at all.

evidence.what: "simple firewall rules or filters based on a single heuristic such as IP addresses are usually not sufficient"; "card testers can create payments and set up cards using your secret key".
evidence.source: Stripe, n.d.
evidence.shows: Refutes the IP-block response and links card testing to key management.

transition_in.introduces: Why the obvious response fails and the worst version.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The controls form a ladder chosen by how much of the checkout the merchant built: keep the hosted checkout, switch on the bot protection and velocity rules already paid for, require a session before a payment, alert on the decline rate, keep a kill switch, and never retry the cards the attacker saved.

evidence.what: Six rungs; Kestrel & Pine's night visible at 23:55 as a 99% decline rate against a usual 4%.
evidence.source: Stripe, n.d.; _research/scenario-ledger.md (incident 8; commerce-security line)
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the controls in order and shows the alert would have fired early.

transition_in.introduces: The layered controls that work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A challenge shown to 2% of genuine shoppers costs more than most card-testing nights, so challenges are triggered by risk signals rather than shown to everyone.

transition_in.carries_over: The ladder's challenges and session requirement.
transition_in.introduces: Why a challenge is triggered by risk rather than shown to everyone.

sections.heading: Account Takeover, Bots and Scraping
sections.controlling_idea: The login, the cart and the catalog are abused at machine speed in the same way as the checkout, and each has its own control: login limits, challenges and change notices, a short cart hold, and a selective scraping policy.

advances_thesis.how: Extends the endpoint controls from the payment form to the login, the cart and the catalog.

transition_in.carries_over: Card testing at the payment form.
transition_in.introduces: The same machine-speed abuse at the login, the cart and the catalog.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Credential stuffing tries passwords leaked elsewhere on the shop's login, and in commerce it ends with an attacker ordering with a customer's saved card to a new address.

evidence.what: "the automated injection of stolen username and password pairs"; MFA as a primary countermeasure.
evidence.source: OWASP, Credential stuffing, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: Defines the attack in OWASP's words.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Customer MFA is rarely enforced because it costs conversion, so three other controls carry the weight against takeover: rate limits and bot management on the login, a challenge for new devices and risky logins, and notification of change.

transition_in.introduces: The controls that stop or catch it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The cart and the catalog are the other doors bots use and are not guarded at the login: inventory hoarding is controlled by the reservation model, and scraping is tolerated selectively (product pages allowed, cart and checkout challenged, the storefront API rate-limited).

transition_in.introduces: The cart and the catalog as further endpoints.

sections.heading: Admin Accounts, Keys and the Apps
sections.controlling_idea: The admin login and the keys of apps and integrations need no other technique, so the merchant gives every person, app and integration its own identity, a narrow key and a named owner who can rotate it.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the merchant's share of responsibility into identities, keys and owners, with Kestrel & Pine's inventory as evidence.

flow.rationale: The admin's value first, then how platforms leave MFA to the merchant, then keys and webhook secrets, then Kestrel & Pine's inventory, then the rule that follows.

transition_in.carries_over: Customer logins attacked by credential stuffing.
transition_in.introduces: Staff logins and the keys of apps and integrations, the bigger target.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Customer logins are one target and staff logins the bigger one: the commerce admin can change the payout account, add checkout scripts, install apps, export customers and issue refunds, so an attacker with it needs no other technique.
Platforms make MFA available but leave enforcement to the merchant, on many plans as a policy to police rather than a switch to flip, and for staff it is never optional.

evidence.what: Staff "can set up two-step authentication for their own individual accounts"; the owner "can't activate two-step authentication for any other staff member"; without it "your payouts might be placed on hold".
evidence.source: Shopify Help Center, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: Shows the merchant, not the platform, deciding whether MFA is enforced.

transition_in.introduces: How one platform handles MFA for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Keys are the other half: no secrets in source code, a vault, restricted least-privilege keys, rotation and audit, any exposure treated as compromise, and a webhook's signing secret treated as a key whose signature check comes before the message is believed.

evidence.what: "bad actors continuously scan public repositories".
evidence.source: Stripe, Best practices for managing secret API keys, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: Shows why a key in a repository is already exposed.

transition_in.introduces: The keys apps and integrations hold.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's January 2027 inventory found 34 integrations, 13 without owners, and 41 apps, three of them writing stock, with five integrations still unowned in April, and each credential needs someone who can explain, limit and replace it.

evidence.what: 34 integrations, 13 without a named owner in January 2027, 5 still unowned in April 2027; 41 apps, 3 with stock-writing permission.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (integration-styles, organizing-commerce-engineering, systems table); consistency-issues ruling 16
evidence.shows: Shows how many keys had nobody to rotate them.

transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine's own count of keys and owners.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's rule is one identity per integration, narrow permissions and a named owner who can rotate its key, recorded in the inventory, because separate identities can be traced and revoked one at a time, narrow permissions limit what a stolen key can change, and an app that asks for more than its job needs is refused at installation.

evidence.what: Figure 4: a key cabinet, 34 integrations, 13 with blank owner tags.
evidence.shows: Shows a key without an owner as one nobody can rotate, scope or trace.

transition_in.introduces: The rule that closes the gap.

sections.heading: Requirements per Control Point
sections.controlling_idea: The controls of the last three sections (the challenge at the payment step, the login limits and the webhook check) sit on the request path and need budgets like any other call: how fast each must answer, how many genuine users it may wrongly stop, what state it keeps, and whether it fails open where another check still stands or closed where it is the only check.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the request-path controls of three sections into engineering requirements with budgets and failure behavior.

transition_in.carries_over: The challenge, login and webhook controls of the last three sections.
transition_in.introduces: The requirements each of them must meet on the request path.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The controls of the last three sections (the challenge at the payment step, the login limits and the webhook check) sit on the request path and need budgets like any other call: how fast each must answer, how many genuine users it may wrongly stop, what state it keeps, and whether it fails open where another check still stands or closed where it is the only check.

evidence.what: Challenge on guest checkout, login rate limit and MFA, webhook signature check: latency, false positives, consistency, failure behavior (figures are assumptions).
evidence.shows: Shows the controls as engineering requirements, not products.

sections.heading: The Choices: Four Security Postures
sections.controlling_idea: Four postures, from platform defaults to a security function, close progressively more of the merchant's share, and the merchant moves one rung when its landscape gains what that rung protects.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the controls into postures with costs and the trigger for each.

transition_in.carries_over: The controls and their requirements, with the inventories of the earlier sections.
transition_in.introduces: How much of them a given merchant should take on, as four postures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four postures, platform defaults, defaults plus paid tools, edge policy and identity management, and a security function, differ in cost, in what they close and leave open, and in when each is right; the last suits a group or a software vendor and is the Giant's Boots for a merchant of Kestrel & Pine's size.

evidence.what: Four postures: cost (illustrative), what each closes and leaves open, when it is right.
evidence.shows: Lets the reader place their merchant on the ladder.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's recommendation is to move up one posture when the landscape gains what that posture protects: the first integration key, the first custom checkout, the first store terminal (a card reader in a shop).

transition_in.introduces: When to move between them.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The controls do not change with scale; the number of identities, keys, scripts and endpoints does, and with it whether anyone can still list them.

advances_thesis.how: Places the postures on the four scale stages with warning signs, including Kestrel & Pine's.

transition_in.introduces: The posture typical of each scale stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Which posture fits depends mostly on the scale stage, and each stage has a typical posture, controls that become necessary and signs that the merchant has outgrown it.

evidence.what: Four stages: typical posture, what becomes necessary, warning signs (Kestrel & Pine's 07:30 pause notice and 13 of 34 unowned integrations in January 2027).
evidence.shows: Shows the same controls growing in number with the stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The shape of the control barely changes with scale; what changes is how many identities, keys, scripts and endpoints there are and whether anyone has a list, which is why an Omnichannel merchant with 34 integrations and 41 apps meets the Lynchpin.

transition_in.introduces: What changes with scale and what does not.

sections.heading: In Practice: Kestrel & Pine's 2027 Security Baseline
sections.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's April 2027 baseline turns every gap of the August night into a control with an owner, and read backwards it would have stopped the night within minutes.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the chapter's controls to one merchant, before and after.

transition_in.carries_over: The posture typical of an Omnichannel merchant.
transition_in.introduces: The posture Kestrel & Pine chose.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In April 2027 Noor Visser and Milan Petrov write a one-page baseline, the second posture plus the parts of the third the integration inventory demands, set against what was true in August 2026.

evidence.what: Eight items before and after: card-data scope, guest checkout, decline alert and kill switch, staff and vendor identity, integration identities, apps (6 unused uninstalled in April and one more by July, stock-write access withdrawn by June, 34 apps in July 2027), checkout scripts, runbooks.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (incident 8; commerce-security line); extensibility-and-app-ecosystems line; consistency-issues rulings 10 and 16
evidence.shows: Shows each control of the chapter adopted with an owner and a date.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read backwards, the baseline stops the Card-Testing Night: the alert fires at 23:55, the challenge stops most attempts, the kill switch ends the rest and a named person is called, because the cost that mattered was the paused account and the raised declines, not the €2,900.

transition_in.introduces: What it would have done on the August night.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Each intrusion has a detection signal and a response in a fixed order, and the merchant that can name its keys and scripts responds narrowly instead of rotating everything.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the runbook outline for each failure.

transition_in.introduces: What to do when an attack gets through anyway.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A card-testing wave is detected by the decline-rate alert and answered with the kill switch, canceled orders, key rotation if the checkout was not the route, weeks of watching the decline rate and no retries of the attacker's cards.

A skimmer found on checkout is removed through whatever loaded it, the evidence is kept and the entry traced, and because card numbers are personal data the incident is also a privacy breach the merchant must report within a deadline, which the next chapter names (72 hours) where it sets out a vendor's duties to the merchant.

transition_in.introduces: The skimmer response.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A compromised admin account or key is revoked first and investigated second, and a merchant that cannot say which integration a leaked key belonged to must rotate everything.

transition_in.introduces: The compromised identity.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Card testing, takeover, skimmers and leaked keys look like four attacks needing four products. Read together they are one gap: every door the chapter examined (the payment form, the login, the cart, the checkout's scripts, the admin and each integration's key) was open by design and worked as the vendor promised; what Kestrel & Pine lacked in August 2026 was a list of its keys and their owners, of the scripts on its checkout, and a signal, the decline rate, that showed the doors being used.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant with those lists sees an attack in the count, closes a door with a setting rather than a deploy, rotates one key rather than all of them, and can sign the SAQ A statement knowing why it is true; one without them learns of the next night from a PSP e-mail in a shared mailbox.

callback.to: The opening's checkout that must accept strangers' payments and Noor Visser's question of which doors are open to a script and who holds each key.
callback.how: p56 answers it with Eva's April 2027 payment set beside one of the 48,000 attempts: the checkout cannot tell them apart one request at a time, but a merchant that watches the decline rate and knows its keys, owners and scripts can.

takeaway.content: Keep the checkout hosted; switch on the controls already paid for; alert on the decline rate beside orders per minute; keep the checkout scripts on a list with owners; give every person, app and integration its own identity and a narrow key with an owner who can rotate it; move one posture rung when the landscape gains what it protects.

hand_off.carries_over: The previous chapter's question of who may act on the shop, answered by a list of identities and keys with owners.
hand_off.introduces: The mirror question about the data the shop holds on people: who may use it, for what and for how long, answered by a list of systems with legal roles, actions and retention clocks.

transition_in.introduces: The chapter's answer to its opening, then what holds, sorted by how settled it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Noor's question has one answer: every door in the chapter was open by design and worked as promised, and Eva's payment and one of the 48,000 attempts look the same to the checkout one request at a time, so they are told apart only in the decline rate, by a merchant that also knows its keys, their owners and its checkout scripts.

evidence.what: The opening checkout and Noor's question set against the sections' controls.
evidence.shows: Answers the opening with what the sections established together.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: keep the card number out of the merchant's systems; the payment page's scripts are the merchant's under 6.4.3, 11.6.1 and the SAQ A statement; card testing and credential stuffing need layered controls; vendors publish the same shared-responsibility line.

evidence.what: Stripe, Adyen, PCI SSC 2024 and 2025, OWASP, Adobe, Shopify.
evidence.shows: Each established point carries its source.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's answer in one paragraph.
transition_in.introduces: What is settled, with sources.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Depends on context: how far up the posture ladder to go, whether to challenge guest checkout given the payment mix, and whether patch cadence or identities deserve the effort, depending on self-hosted or SaaS.

transition_in.introduces: What depends on the merchant's situation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: for a merchant renting its platform, security is an inventory problem before a technology problem, and the decline rate belongs beside orders per minute on the dashboard.

transition_in.introduces: The author's own judgement.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eight questions turn the chapter into a review of the reader's own shop: the SAQ and attestations, the checkout's scripts, unprotected endpoints, enforced MFA, identities and keys per integration, who would notice a PSP pause, the decline rate and kill switch, and app scopes.

transition_in.introduces: Questions the reader can ask of its own shop.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Security decides who may act on the shop; the next chapter asks the mirror question about the data the shop holds on people: who may use it, for what and for how long.

transition_in.carries_over: Who may act on the shop, answered by a list of identities and keys with owners.
transition_in.introduces: The mirror question about the data held on people.
